reading.title: The repair library
reading.text:
A. In the fictional town of Arden, a library began lending tools in 2018. Its first collection contained forty items donated by residents. The service was created because many people needed a drill for a single afternoon but could not justify buying one. Rather than treating borrowing as a substitute for all ownership, the organisers focused on equipment used infrequently. Books remained the library's principal activity, and the new service occupied a former storage room.
B. Borrowers attended a safety session before receiving a membership card. Membership cost twelve pounds per year, while individual loans were free. A tool could normally be kept for seven days. Gardening equipment was especially popular in spring, whereas decorating tools were borrowed throughout the year. Volunteers inspected returned items and recorded damage. They did not assume that a clean appearance proved a machine was safe.
C. A small evaluation compared interviews with loan records. Interviews suggested that people valued saving money, but records showed another pattern: neighbours often borrowed equipment together. The researcher, Mara Ellis, argued that the library also created opportunities for conversation. However, she warned that interviewees who enjoyed the service might be more willing to participate than disappointed users. The evaluation did not estimate the programme's carbon savings.
D. Demand created a practical difficulty. Several borrowers wanted the same machines on Saturdays, although those machines remained unused on weekdays. The library introduced reservations rather than purchasing a second copy of every item. A text message reminded members when equipment was due. Late returns fell after the reminders began, but the evaluation could not separate the effect of messages from the effect of a new volunteer coordinator.
E. A repair workshop followed the lending scheme. Participants brought broken household objects and worked beside experienced volunteers. The workshop required visitors to remain involved rather than simply leave an object for someone else to fix. Some repairs failed because replacement components were unavailable. Organisers considered such failures useful if participants learned how an object worked. They rejected the claim that every damaged product could be restored economically.
F. The library's example illustrates the difference between access and capability. Lending a tool gives a resident access to equipment; explaining safe use develops capability. Combining the two can broaden participation, but staff time is a real cost. The fictional study therefore recommends gradual expansion and careful records rather than an immediate promise to offer every household appliance.
G. For the repair library, ownership was not simply a financial decision. A resident might prefer to own an item because it was immediately available, because they knew its condition, or because borrowing involved travel. The organisers therefore asked which obstacles prevented people from using the service. A long opening period was of little value to someone who could not carry a heavy tool home. Conversely, a delivery arrangement could be expensive even if it increased access. Evaluating participation meant examining the whole journey from hearing about the collection to returning an item, rather than counting a membership card as proof of meaningful use.
H. Records of maintenance were designed to support decisions, not to identify careless members automatically. A worn component could result from ordinary use, an existing defect or poor instruction. Staff recorded what they observed and separated that observation from assumptions about responsibility. This was particularly important when a member reported a problem voluntarily. Punishing every such report might encourage people to hide damage, making the collection less safe. The library instead treated early reporting as useful information. Where misuse was suspected, a volunteer discussed what had happened and checked whether the safety guidance had been clear enough for the borrower.
I. Reservations also introduced questions of fairness. Giving priority to the first online request might disadvantage a resident who could not use the website. Staff therefore accepted requests in person and by telephone as well. They explained the reservation rules publicly and kept a waiting list when demand exceeded supply. Such arrangements did not remove scarcity, but they made the process more understandable. The team regarded complaints as opportunities to inspect the rules rather than evidence that the entire project had failed. Some disagreements concerned genuine conflicts between equally reasonable needs, which no booking system could resolve without making a choice.
J. Finally, the organisers distinguished the success of an individual repair from the success of a learning programme. A repaired kettle might stop working again, while a visitor whose object could not be fixed might still gain confidence in asking informed questions. Both outcomes mattered, but they required different evidence. Follow-up conversations could reveal whether participants used a skill later, although those conversations depended on people responding. The report describes this limitation openly. It concludes that a community service should make modest claims supported by its records, while remaining willing to revise its methods when residents identify needs that those records overlook.

reading.title: Shade and city streets
reading.text:
A. The fictional city of Bellhaven studied heat on two neighbouring streets. One had mature trees; the other had recently been rebuilt with a pale pavement. Engineers initially expected the new surface to perform best because it reflected more sunlight. Residents, however, described walking under trees as more comfortable. The project investigated why a surface-temperature measurement might not fully explain a pedestrian's experience.
B. Sensors were placed at the same height on both streets. Measurements were taken at noon and again after sunset for six weeks. Researchers also recorded cloud cover and wind speed. They avoided comparing a cloudy afternoon on one street with a clear afternoon on the other. Nevertheless, the streets differed in building height, so the team could not attribute every difference to trees or pavement alone.
C. The pale pavement had a lower surface temperature at noon. Yet it reflected sunlight towards people standing nearby. Under the trees, shade reduced direct radiation reaching pedestrians. The team distinguished air temperature from radiant heat: a person may feel warmer even when the air around them has not changed much. This distinction explained why the coolest measured surface was not necessarily the most comfortable place to walk.
D. After sunset, both streets released stored energy. The trees did not make this release disappear. Buildings and roads contributed to the evening warmth, and the researchers did not measure indoor conditions. Project leader Ishan Vale described trees as one component of a wider strategy. He opposed presenting a single intervention as a cure for every urban heat problem.
E. Maintenance complicated the comparison. The reflective surface required cleaning, while young trees needed watering during dry periods. The council's original budget included installation but excluded these continuing costs. A revised estimate added maintenance over ten years. Residents also asked who would receive the improvements first. A technically efficient plan could still be unfair if it concentrated shade in already comfortable neighbourhoods.
F. The report recommends selecting interventions according to local conditions and human needs. A narrow street may not have space for large trees, while a busy square may benefit greatly from shade. Combining measurements with resident experience does not mean abandoning science. It means defining the outcome carefully. Comfort, surface temperature, cost and access are related, but they are not interchangeable measures.
G. Pedestrian comfort also depends on the activity being performed. A person waiting at a bus stop may remain exposed in one location, whereas someone walking quickly passes through a sequence of sunny and shaded areas. Measuring a single point cannot represent both experiences equally well. The Bellhaven team therefore drew walking routes and noted where people were likely to pause. These observations helped the council identify places where a small shaded area could be valuable. They did not replace temperature measurements; rather, they clarified the situations in which those measurements would be interpreted and the decisions they were intended to inform.
H. Tree selection raised further questions. A species suitable for one street might grow poorly where roots have little space or where underground services constrain planting. Large canopies provide shade, but their development takes time. Young trees require protection and care before residents experience the promised benefits. Treating the purchase price as the entire cost would hide this period of establishment. The report also warns against assuming that all residents value the same streetscape. Some may emphasise clear sightlines, while others prioritise shade or habitat. Design discussions need to address these concerns through specific arrangements rather than presenting them as a simple conflict between science and preference.
I. The team considered how a result should be communicated. Saying that a treatment reduced temperature invites the question of which temperature, at what time and under what conditions. A surface measurement cannot automatically be translated into a claim about health, indoor comfort or energy bills. Those outcomes would require additional evidence. A clear report therefore names the measure and describes its limitations beside the result. This does not make the finding less useful. It makes it easier for another district to judge whether the conditions resemble its own and whether the same intervention deserves a trial there.
J. Planning under uncertainty is still planning. The council could begin with a limited intervention, monitor maintenance demands and consult users before expanding it. Such an approach leaves room to correct an unsuitable choice without abandoning the wider objective. It also makes responsibilities explicit: someone must inspect the surface, maintain trees and respond when residents report problems. Without these arrangements, a promising design may deteriorate after installation. The fictional comparison ultimately shows that effective heat adaptation requires a connection between technical evidence, continuing practical work and the everyday circumstances of the people whose comfort the project is intended to improve.

reading.title: When predictions change behaviour
reading.text:
A. A forecast is usually evaluated by comparing a prediction with a later event. This appears straightforward when the object being studied cannot hear the forecast. Announcing rain does not make clouds disappear. Social forecasts are different: people may respond to an announcement and change the outcome. The following argument uses invented examples to explain that difficulty rather than reporting a real experiment.
B. Suppose a transport agency predicts severe congestion on a bridge. Drivers hear the warning and choose other routes. Traffic on the bridge then remains manageable. An observer might call the prediction inaccurate, yet the announcement helped prevent the predicted event. Descriptive accuracy and practical effect must therefore be distinguished. A useful warning can fail to describe what eventually happens precisely because it is useful.
C. The opposite process is also possible. A rumour predicts a shortage of a household product. Customers buy unusually large quantities, creating the shortage they fear. Here the announcement helps produce the event rather than prevent it. Researchers call this a self-fulfilling process. They should still investigate supply conditions instead of assuming that every shortage originates in a rumour.
D. To study these mechanisms, an evaluator needs a credible comparison. One approach compares groups that received a warning with similar groups that did not. But messages may spread between groups, weakening the separation. Another approach uses earlier periods as a baseline. That method is limited when population, prices or weather have changed. There is no comparison method that automatically removes every source of uncertainty.
E. Philosopher Lena Hart argues that evaluators should state the purpose of a forecast before selecting a measure. A warning designed to reduce harm should be assessed partly through avoided harm, not just prediction error. Analyst Owen Reed agrees that purposes matter but warns against allowing any unsuccessful forecast to be declared a hidden success. A causal claim requires evidence of changed behaviour, not an attractive story added afterwards.
F. These arguments support careful evaluation rather than abandonment of evaluation. Researchers can examine who received a message, what actions followed and whether plausible alternatives explain the outcome. They should report uncertainty and separate observation from inference. A forecast about social behaviour is not merely a picture of the future; it may become part of the process that produces that future.
G. The timing of an announcement adds another complication. A forecast issued early may give people enough time to respond, but it may also be based on less complete information. A later forecast can be more precise while arriving too late to prevent harm. Evaluators should therefore consider the decision available at the time rather than judging an announcement only with knowledge obtained afterwards. This distinction does not excuse careless prediction. It asks whether the evidence reasonably supported the warning and whether the proposed response was proportionate to the risk as it could then be understood.
H. Communication changes the mechanism as well. Some people may read a numerical estimate as a guarantee, while others may interpret it as one possibility among several. A message that explains uncertainty can help recipients understand why a predicted event may not occur. Yet an explanation that is too complicated may not reach people who need to act quickly. The problem is not solved simply by adding more detail. The agency must identify the audience, the action being requested and the consequences of misunderstanding. Testing how people interpret a warning can reveal difficulties that are invisible when analysts inspect the numbers alone.
I. Distribution matters when a forecast affects several groups. Drivers diverted from a bridge may reduce congestion there while increasing traffic on residential streets. Calling the intervention successful on the basis of the bridge alone would ignore these transferred effects. A broader evaluation asks who benefits, who bears a cost and whether the response creates a new problem elsewhere. This may require combining transport measurements with accounts from residents. Such accounts are evidence about experience, not automatic proof of a causal effect. They help identify outcomes that should be measured and alternative explanations that deserve investigation.
J. Researchers can also document their evaluation plan before an outcome is known. A plan specifies which observations would support the proposed mechanism and which would count against it. This reduces the temptation to invent a favourable interpretation for any result. The plan may still need revision if an unexpected event occurs, but the revision should be explained rather than hidden. Evaluating social predictions is therefore demanding because forecasts can interact with behaviour, communication and competing interests. Recognising those interactions makes evaluation more rigorous. It does not mean that every failed prediction was secretly effective or that a warning should be judged only by whether people found it reassuring.

writing.prompt: The table shows the percentages of commuters using buses and bicycles in fictional City 1 in three years. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
writing.plan: Introduce the measures and years. Give an overview of both trends. Compare the beginning and end, then support comparisons with figures.
writing.model:
The table compares the proportions of commuters travelling by bus and bicycle in a fictional city in 2010, 2015 and 2020. Overall, both forms of transport became more common, but buses remained the more widely used option throughout the period. The increase in cycling was larger in percentage-point terms.

In 2010, buses accounted for 30% of commuters, compared with 10% for bicycles. By 2015, the bus figure had risen to 45%, while cycling reached 20%. This left a gap of 25 percentage points between the two modes in the middle year.

By 2020, the share using buses stood at 50%, representing an overall rise of 20 percentage points. Bicycle use reached 35%, an increase of 25 points from its initial level. Consequently, the difference between the two modes narrowed from 20 points in 2010 to 15 points in 2020. These figures describe separate proportions and do not imply that the categories represent all commuting methods.

writing.prompt: Cities should invest more in public libraries than in entertainment facilities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
writing.plan: Define your position and two main reasons. Plan one claim, explanation and example per body paragraph. Address the exact task and conclude without a new argument.
writing.model:
Public libraries deserve substantial investment because they support education and provide access to services that many residents cannot obtain privately. However, I do not think that cities should neglect entertainment entirely. A sensible policy gives libraries reliable funding while assessing other facilities according to their public value.

One reason to prioritise libraries is that their benefits reach beyond borrowing books. Students can use quiet study areas, job seekers can access information, and residents can attend affordable learning activities. For example, a library that lends equipment and teaches basic repair skills can reduce the cost of learning a practical activity. These services are especially valuable to people whose homes lack space or resources. Investment should therefore include trained staff as well as buildings.

Nevertheless, entertainment facilities can also serve the community. A public theatre or sports centre may provide opportunities for social contact, exercise and cultural participation. The question is whether the facility is accessible and whether its benefits justify the cost. A very expensive venue used by a small group should not automatically receive priority over a widely used library. Conversely, a modest recreation space in an underserved neighbourhood may be an excellent investment.

Cities should therefore compare needs rather than treat every library as beneficial and every entertainment project as unnecessary. They can examine likely users, operating costs and barriers to access before allocating funds. Public consultation can reveal needs that a simple attendance forecast misses. In my view, libraries should receive a strong funding foundation, but the remaining budget should support a balanced range of services that residents can realistically use.

reading.title: Seeds in storage
reading.text:
A. The fictional Lark Research Centre stores seeds to protect plant diversity. Its collection began with locally grown beans but later included wild plants from coastal habitats. Collectors record the location and date of each sample. A seed without reliable background information may still grow, yet it is less useful for researchers studying how populations differ. The centre treats documentation as part of the collection, not an optional extra.
B. Many seeds are dried before they enter cold storage. Lower moisture slows chemical reactions that damage cells. Staff place prepared seeds in sealed containers at minus eighteen degrees Celsius. However, not every species tolerates drying. Some tropical plants require other conservation methods. The centre therefore rejects the assumption that one storage procedure is appropriate for all plants.
C. Stored seeds are tested periodically. A small sample is placed under conditions suitable for germination, and the proportion that grows is recorded. If viability declines below an agreed threshold, staff plan a new collection or grow plants to produce fresh seeds. Germination is not equivalent to long-term health: a seedling can emerge and then fail. Records include later observations where possible.
D. Growing replacement plants introduces its own risk. If only a few individuals reproduce, the next generation may represent less genetic variation than the original sample. Researchers try to grow enough plants and prevent unintended mixing. They also consider whether greenhouse conditions favour traits that were not common in the wild. Conservation can alter the very material it aims to preserve.
E. Community relationships matter as much as laboratory equipment. Local growers may know when a plant produces mature seeds or which fields contain an unusual variety. The centre requests permission before collecting and explains how material may be used. It does not promise that a stored sample will automatically produce a profitable new crop. Benefits and access require explicit discussion.
F. Seed storage is therefore an active process involving monitoring, records and decisions. A sealed container is only one part of conservation. Protecting habitats remains necessary because plants interact with soils, insects and climate. A collection can provide a safeguard, but it cannot reproduce every relationship that keeps a living population functioning.
G. The centre also distinguishes a sample from the population it represents. Collecting seeds from a convenient roadside patch may be easier than reaching a remote valley, but convenience can shape the collection. A population may vary across soil conditions, elevation or flowering time. Recording where material was collected allows later users to understand some of these limits. It does not guarantee that every kind of variation was captured. The team therefore describes its sampling decisions and avoids presenting a small collection as a complete representation of all plants in a region. The value of the material depends partly on knowing what it cannot represent.
H. Decisions about testing must balance information against the use of finite material. Germinating seeds provides evidence about viability, but it also removes seeds from the stored sample. Testing too rarely risks discovering deterioration late; testing unnecessarily often can reduce a small collection. Staff consider the amount available, previous results and the biology of the species when deciding how to proceed. A numerical threshold is a practical guide rather than a claim that all seeds below it have become worthless. Even a weakened sample may retain information or genetic characteristics that would be difficult to replace through a new collection.
I. Digital records make a collection easier to search, but they introduce their own maintenance requirements. A location entered under two different spellings can appear to describe two places. A date without an explanation may refer to collection, preparation or testing. The centre uses clear field definitions and records corrections rather than silently overwriting uncertain information. Researchers who combine data from several institutions need these conventions to interpret a record correctly. A database is useful because it organises evidence; it should not make a precise-looking entry appear more certain than the observation on which it was based.
J. Finally, conservation priorities involve choices. A well-known crop may attract funding because its practical value is immediately visible, while a less familiar wild plant may be overlooked. Staff can explain the reasons for protecting different species, but they cannot remove every disagreement about limited resources. Communities may value cultural uses, researchers may emphasise rare traits, and land managers may focus on habitat relationships. An effective programme makes these reasons visible and reviews its priorities as knowledge changes. Cold storage can support that programme, but its technical reliability should not conceal the social decisions that determine which plants enter the collection and who can use them later.

reading.title: Learning through retrieval
reading.text:
A. In a fictional education study, students read a short science text and then followed one of two activities. One group reread the text; the other closed it and wrote down what they remembered. The second activity is known as retrieval practice. It requires learners to reconstruct information rather than simply encounter it again. The study examined both immediate confidence and later performance.
B. Students who reread reported greater confidence immediately afterwards. The material felt familiar and was easy to follow while visible. Students using retrieval practice often noticed gaps and felt less certain. A test one week later nevertheless favoured the retrieval group. The researchers argued that ease during study and durability of learning are different outcomes, although neither activity guarantees success for every learner.
C. Feedback was an important condition. After recalling the text, students checked their responses against it and corrected errors. Without feedback, a learner might repeatedly practise an inaccurate version. Teacher Amira Stone described retrieval as a tool for discovering what needs attention. She did not recommend turning every learning activity into a high-pressure examination.
D. The experiment used short factual material and a limited sample. It did not establish that the same procedure would work equally well for practical skills or complex arguments. Students had volunteered, which could make them more motivated than other learners. The authors reported these limitations rather than extending the results to every classroom.
E. Timing also matters. A learner may recall an answer immediately after reading without forming a durable memory. Leaving a gap between study and retrieval can make the exercise more demanding. The appropriate gap depends on the learner and the intended retention period. The report does not prescribe a universal interval such as exactly twenty-four hours.
F. A balanced study routine can combine explanation, examples, retrieval and correction. Familiarity should not be confused with mastery, but difficulty should not be celebrated for its own sake. A task is useful when it directs attention to relevant knowledge and supports improvement. The fictional study's central lesson is to judge methods by what learners retain and can use, rather than how effortless a study session feels.
G. Retrieval questions should match the intended learning outcome. Recalling an isolated term can be useful when the term itself matters, but it is not sufficient when a learner needs to compare arguments or apply a principle. A teacher can ask students to explain why an example fits a concept or to identify evidence for a conclusion. These tasks demand more than repeating a definition. They also make marking more complex, because different wording may express the same idea. Feedback should therefore focus on meaning and reasoning rather than treating a single memorised sentence as the only acceptable response.
H. Learners differ in the knowledge they bring to a task. A question that prompts productive effort in one student may leave another unable to begin. In that situation, an example or a brief explanation can make retrieval possible. The goal is not to maximise struggle but to establish a useful sequence of attempt, feedback and another attempt. As understanding improves, support can be reduced. This makes the activity responsive to evidence about the learner rather than fixed to a label such as easy or difficult. It also explains why a technique that worked in one short study cannot simply be imposed unchanged on every class.
I. Confidence can still provide useful information if it is compared with performance. A student who is certain of a wrong answer needs a different kind of review from one who knows that they are unsure. Asking learners to state their confidence before seeing feedback can reveal this difference. However, confidence should not replace assessment of the answer itself. Some students express certainty readily, while others hesitate even when they understand. The teacher can use the comparison to guide discussion, but should avoid interpreting a personality difference as proof of stronger or weaker knowledge.
J. The fictional study also encourages learners to record errors in a practical way. A notebook can include the original question, the mistaken response, the corrected explanation and a new example. Reviewing that notebook is useful only if the learner eventually tries to answer without looking at the correction. Otherwise, the correction itself may merely become familiar. A later attempt provides fresh evidence of what can be recalled or applied. Good study planning therefore includes both support and checks. Its success is measured by increasing independence and accurate use of knowledge, rather than the number of pages reread or the reassuring feeling that a topic has been encountered many times.

reading.title: The value of silence in archives
reading.text:
A. An archive contains surviving records, not a complete copy of the past. Historian Nila Ford illustrates this distinction with a fictional factory collection. The archive holds managers' reports and equipment purchases but few workers' letters. A researcher who counts documents without considering how they survived may mistake the most visible group for the only important group.
B. Records can be absent for several reasons. Some activities were never written down; other documents were lost or deliberately destroyed. Storage costs may have led an organisation to keep financial papers while discarding routine conversations. These mechanisms are different. The absence of a document does not, by itself, identify which mechanism operated.
C. Ford compares the factory records with newspaper reports and oral interviews. A newspaper may reveal a dispute omitted from official minutes, while an interview can explain daily working practices. Neither source is automatically superior. Journalists select stories, and memories can change. The researcher asks what each source can reasonably support and where independent evidence is needed.
D. Analyst Tomas Lee proposes digitising every surviving page to improve access. Ford welcomes wider access but questions the word every. Fragile material may require conservation before scanning, and personal information may need restrictions. Digitisation changes availability; it does not remove gaps or guarantee that an image can be interpreted correctly. Search tools can favour clearly printed names over handwritten ones.
E. The team records uncertain interpretations separately from confirmed facts. For example, a missing wage sheet might suggest interrupted record-keeping, but it cannot prove that workers received no wages. The distinction resembles the difference between a contradiction and a lack of evidence. Responsible historical writing makes that boundary visible rather than filling every gap with a confident narrative.
F. Archives remain valuable precisely because their limits can be investigated. Researchers can compare collections, describe selection processes and revisit conclusions when new material appears. Silence is not meaningless, but its meaning requires argument. The goal is neither blind trust in documents nor total scepticism; it is an account whose claims remain proportionate to the evidence.
G. Cataloguing decisions influence what a visitor can find. If records are arranged only under the names of senior managers, a search for an ordinary worker may return nothing even when that person appears inside a document. Describing a collection at several levels can improve discovery, but detailed cataloguing requires time. The archive explains the level of description available and invites researchers to consult related material. An unsuccessful search is consequently not the same as proof that a topic is absent. It may reflect the terms used, the description of the collection or the limits of a particular search tool.
H. Material condition can also shape interpretation. A torn page may preserve a conclusion while losing the passage that qualified it. An ink stain may obscure a date without hiding the rest of a letter. Researchers should record these difficulties instead of completing a gap with the most convenient guess. They may compare another copy, examine surrounding entries or leave the matter unresolved. Uncertainty is not always a weakness in an account. When the source is incomplete, clearly identifying uncertainty can be more accurate than producing a smooth narrative that implies knowledge the document does not actually supply.
I. Oral interviews raise questions of context similar to those raised by written records. An interviewee may describe an event differently depending on the question, the audience or the time available. A researcher can preserve the interview conditions and distinguish the speaker's recollection from independently confirmed chronology. This does not make personal testimony unimportant. It can illuminate values, experiences and meanings that an administrative document never attempted to record. The strongest interpretation often comes from understanding why sources differ, rather than selecting one source as completely reliable and dismissing the rest.
J. Access policies require explanation too. Restricting a document containing personal information may protect living people, while excessive restriction can prevent legitimate research. An archive can publish the reasons for its policy and identify when a restriction may be reviewed. It should also distinguish between material that is closed, material that has not yet been described and material known to be missing. These categories produce different consequences for a researcher. The fictional factory case therefore extends beyond the reading of individual pages. It asks how preservation, cataloguing and access together shape the evidence available, and how a responsible researcher can describe those conditions without treating every silence as an answer.

writing.prompt: The chart and table show the numbers of books borrowed from a fictional college library in three categories in 2015 and 2025. Summarise the main features and make comparisons where relevant.
writing.plan: Introduce the measures and years. Give an overview of both trends. Compare the beginning and end, then support comparisons with figures.
writing.model:
The chart compares the numbers of science, history and literature books borrowed from a fictional college library in 2015 and 2025. Overall, borrowing increased in science and literature, while history was the only category to decline. Science remained the most frequently borrowed category in both years.

In 2015, 120 science books were borrowed, compared with 100 history books and 80 literature books. Thus, the difference between the highest and lowest categories was 40 books. Ten years later, science borrowing reached 180, representing an increase of 60 books. Literature rose more sharply, from 80 to 150, a gain of 70 books.

By contrast, the number of history books borrowed fell from 100 to 90. This placed history below literature in 2025, whereas their order had been reversed in 2015. Total borrowing across the three categories increased from 300 to 420 books. The figures therefore show both an overall rise in borrowing and a change in the relative popularity of the subjects. They do not provide information about the reasons for these changes.

writing.prompt: Some people think students should study alone, while others favour collaborative learning. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
writing.plan: Define your position and two main reasons. Plan one claim, explanation and example per body paragraph. Address the exact task and conclude without a new argument.
writing.model:
Studying alone and learning with others offer different advantages. Independent study can improve concentration, while collaboration can reveal misunderstandings and encourage learners to explain their ideas. I believe that students benefit most from combining the two, with the balance determined by the task.

Those who favour studying alone often value control over time and pace. A learner can spend longer on a difficult passage without waiting for a group or feeling embarrassed. Independent retrieval practice also shows what the student can remember without assistance. For instance, closing a textbook and writing a short explanation can expose gaps that would be hidden if another person supplied the answer. A quiet environment is therefore useful for both concentration and honest self-assessment.

Collaborative learning provides a different kind of feedback. Students must express their understanding clearly, and a partner may question an assumption that initially seemed obvious. Comparing two explanations of the same sentence can reveal an important difference in meaning. However, group work is less useful if one participant completes the task while the others remain passive. Teachers should assign roles and ensure that everyone contributes rather than assume that sitting together produces learning.

In my view, students should first make an individual attempt and then discuss selected problems. They can return to independent work afterwards to check whether they can apply the explanation themselves. This sequence preserves personal responsibility while taking advantage of other perspectives. It also avoids making collaboration a substitute for effort. Ultimately, neither method is universally superior: effective study requires choosing an approach that supports the intended learning outcome and checking whether understanding has actually improved.

reading.title: Wetlands beside the railway
reading.text:
A. In the invented district of Mossbridge, a railway embankment separated a wetland from a seasonal stream. During heavy rain, water accumulated on one side and nearby roads flooded. Engineers proposed a larger drain, while ecologists suggested restoring the connection between stream and wetland. The council commissioned a comparison rather than assuming that either proposal would solve every problem.
B. The wetland could temporarily hold water, allowing it to reach the stream more slowly. This storage function depended on available capacity: saturated ground could absorb less additional water. The team measured water levels before and after storms. It did not claim that wetlands prevent all flooding, especially during unusually intense rainfall.
C. A trial used two adjustable openings under the railway. Staff kept one narrow during the first month and widened it later. Water movement increased after widening, but rainfall also differed between months. The researchers therefore treated the trial as evidence about feasibility rather than a precise estimate of the effect under identical conditions.
D. Maintenance workers worried that plant debris would block the openings. Ecologist Rosa Malik agreed that inspection was necessary and recommended removable screens. She opposed clearing every plant from the wetland because vegetation supported habitat and slowed water. Engineer Felix Ward focused on safe access for staff. Their recommendations differed in emphasis but both included maintenance.
E. The restoration created a walking route with raised sections. Residents welcomed access but asked the council to protect quiet areas used by birds. A visitor survey found support for guided walks, yet it included only people already using the route. The authors cautioned that residents unable to reach the site were underrepresented.
F. The final proposal combined water monitoring, scheduled inspection and limited public access. It also included a review after two wet seasons. The project illustrates why infrastructure and ecosystems should be considered together. Restoring a connection changes flows, habitat and human use; evaluating only one of these outcomes would leave important effects unseen.
G. Water management operates across a landscape rather than within a single boundary. An intervention near the railway may influence land upstream or downstream. The council therefore mapped likely connections before selecting the trial location. These maps represented a working understanding, not an assurance that every flow had been identified. Heavy rain can reveal routes that are rarely visible in dry weather. Observations from maintenance staff and nearby residents helped the team decide where to inspect after a storm. Their reports were compared with measurements so that an isolated observation did not automatically become a general conclusion.
H. The walking route created a second set of practical decisions. Raised sections could protect visitors from shallow water, but they needed surfaces that remained usable when wet. Signs also had to distinguish a temporary closure from a permanent restriction. Without clear information, visitors might attempt an unsafe shortcut or assume that the whole site was inaccessible. Planning public access therefore involved more than installing a path. It required decisions about inspection, communication and responsibility when conditions changed. The team included these activities in its operating plan instead of treating them as problems to be solved only after the route opened.
I. Habitat monitoring raised the issue of seasonal variation. Fewer birds observed during one visit might reflect the time of year, the weather or the observer's position. It could not immediately be attributed to visitors. Ecologists recorded the conditions of each observation and compared repeated visits where possible. They also considered whether public access might be concentrated in some areas while quieter areas remained protected. This approach did not assume that any human presence was harmless or that all access should be forbidden. It sought evidence about particular patterns of use and their consequences.
J. Funding arrangements affected what could be sustained. An opening grant might pay for construction while leaving inspection and repairs dependent on a later budget. A design that looked affordable at installation could therefore create an ongoing burden. The council considered who would perform each task and how problems would be reported. Residents were invited to describe their experience, but reporting was not treated as a replacement for professional inspection. The proposal's strength lay in connecting ecological goals with practical responsibilities. Restoring water movement was the beginning of a managed process, not the end of the council's obligations to nearby residents, railway users and the people visiting the wetland.

reading.title: Measuring work beyond output
reading.text:
A. A fictional design cooperative compared two ways of evaluating teams. The first counted completed assignments; the second considered completion alongside rework, staff learning and client needs. Counting output was simple, but the cooperative suspected that a single total could reward hurried work. The experiment was intended to improve internal decisions, not rank every organisation.
B. Managers noticed that teams working on familiar projects completed more assignments. Teams handling novel problems produced fewer finished items but developed reusable methods. A comparison that ignored task difficulty would confuse different kinds of work. The cooperative recorded project complexity before examining results, although these ratings still involved judgement.
C. Rework provided another clue. Some assignments were marked complete and then returned for revision. The revised system tracked these returns rather than deleting them from the original count. Designer Mei Carter argued that a successful handover requires work the client can use. Analyst Bruno Hale warned that a demanding client might request revisions even when the original work was competent.
D. Staff learning was measured through documented reflections and later demonstrations. A reflection alone could be written to satisfy managers, so the team looked for evidence that a new method was used. It did not assign a monetary value to every learning activity. Some benefits appeared only after several months and could not be attributed to a single training session.
E. Introducing new indicators changed behaviour. Teams began keeping better records, but some spent time preparing attractive reports rather than improving their processes. The cooperative reduced reporting requirements and used periodic conversations to check examples. No indicator was considered immune to strategic presentation once it became a target.
F. The study concludes that several measures can improve understanding, provided they are interpreted rather than simply added together. A large dashboard is not automatically a good evaluation. The relevant question is which decision each measure helps someone make. When the work changes, the measures may need revision too.
G. Measures are easier to interpret when their purpose is stated. If a completion total is used to plan staffing, the cooperative needs to know how much work remains and how difficult it is likely to be. If the same total is used to reward employees, it may encourage people to select easier assignments or mark work complete too early. A number that is useful for one decision can therefore be misleading for another. The team discussed the intended decision before changing a measure. It also avoided assuming that collecting more data would automatically solve a disagreement about what good work meant.
H. Comparison over time introduces another challenge. A team may improve while facing more demanding projects, so its completion total can remain stable. Alternatively, a simpler mix of tasks may create the appearance of improvement without any change in skill. The cooperative examined examples of work beside the totals to understand these possibilities. Examples require interpretation and can be selected strategically, so managers asked how each example had been chosen. This question helped them distinguish a typical case from an unusually successful demonstration. No single technique removed the need for judgement, but making the selection process visible improved the discussion.
I. Employees needed to understand the revised system. If they believed that an indicator would determine promotion on its own, they might focus on that indicator even when managers intended it only as a starting point for conversation. The cooperative explained how evidence would be used and allowed staff to question a record. Corrections were retained so that changes could be understood later. Transparency did not eliminate anxiety or disagreement, but it reduced uncertainty about the procedure. It also revealed places where managers had used the same term to mean different things, which required clarification before fair comparisons were possible.
J. The experiment encourages organisations to distinguish monitoring from explanation. A dashboard can show that returns increased; it cannot by itself identify whether the cause was rushed work, a new client requirement or a more thorough inspection. Acting on an assumed cause may create another problem. Managers should therefore use an indicator to ask a focused question and then examine relevant evidence. This takes more effort than responding automatically to a coloured warning, but it makes intervention more likely to address the actual issue. The cooperative's final recommendation is a small set of interpretable measures, supported by examples and open to revision when the work or the decisions change.

reading.title: Translation and shared understanding
reading.text:
A. A fictional international research group adopted a shared vocabulary for its meetings. Members spoke different first languages, and an English term could carry slightly different associations for each person. The group discovered that agreeing on a word did not always mean agreeing on a concept. It began recording examples alongside definitions.
B. One disagreement concerned the word efficient. An engineer used it to describe energy consumption, while an administrator used it to describe staff time. Both meanings were reasonable within their contexts. A translator who selected a familiar equivalent without asking about the intended measure could preserve the word while losing the practical distinction.
C. The group tested a glossary in two workshops. In the first, participants received definitions alone; in the second, they received definitions with short scenarios. Participants in the second workshop identified more misunderstandings. However, the workshops had different members, so the researchers did not treat this result as definitive proof that scenarios caused the improvement.
D. Linguist Sara Lin recommends checking understanding through paraphrase. Asking a participant to explain a concept in another way can reveal differences hidden by repeated terminology. She distinguishes this from forcing everyone to use identical sentences. Variation in expression may be compatible with shared meaning, while identical expression may conceal disagreement.
E. Coordinator David Moss raises a practical concern: lengthy clarification can slow a meeting. Lin accepts the cost but argues that unresolved ambiguity may create greater delays later. The group therefore prioritised terms linked to decisions rather than discussing every possible linguistic difference. Meeting notes included unresolved questions as well as agreements.
F. Shared understanding emerged through a process of explanation, examples and revision. The glossary remained a working document rather than a final authority. Translation was treated as a cooperative task, not merely replacing one label with another. The fictional case suggests that communication quality depends on making assumptions visible and checking consequences, as well as choosing accurate words.
G. The group found that definitions become more useful when their boundaries are explored. An example shows a case that fits a term, while a contrasting example shows a nearby case that does not. Together they help participants understand why a distinction matters. The glossary therefore included situations in which a label would be misleading. Such material took time to prepare, but it could be reused when new members joined. The group treated that effort as part of collaboration rather than a separate administrative burden. It still checked understanding in meetings, because reading a document did not guarantee that every participant interpreted it in the intended way.
H. A shared language can create an uneven burden. A fluent speaker may explain an idea quickly, while another participant needs more time to formulate the same point. Silence may therefore reflect the pace of a discussion rather than a lack of knowledge. The coordinator introduced pauses and invited written comments after meetings. This did not require lowering the standard of an argument. It created more than one opportunity to present an argument clearly. The team remained attentive to whether decisions were being shaped mainly by those who could respond fastest, rather than by the strength of the evidence each person could contribute.
I. Paraphrase also needs to be used carefully. A listener who says the same sentence in slightly different words may still be repeating an unexplored assumption. Asking for an example or a predicted consequence can provide a stronger check. For instance, participants can discuss what a proposed definition would imply for a practical decision. If their predictions differ, the apparent agreement deserves further discussion. The aim is not to remove all variation in interpretation. It is to identify the variation that matters for the work being planned and to prevent a superficial verbal agreement from being mistaken for a settled decision.
J. Finally, the glossary had a revision history. When a term changed, members could see why the new description had been adopted and which earlier documents used the previous version. Without that history, an old report might appear inconsistent with a later meeting even if both had used the vocabulary accepted at the time. Recording changes made communication more traceable. It also reinforced the idea that a glossary is a tool serving a group, not an authority that cannot be questioned. Shared understanding developed through repeated checks, respectful clarification and attention to practical consequences, with terminology supporting that process rather than replacing it.

writing.prompt: The pie chart and table show the distribution of a fictional city council energy-efficiency budget in 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
writing.plan: Introduce the measures and years. Give an overview of both trends. Compare the beginning and end, then support comparisons with figures.
writing.model:
The pie chart shows how a fictional city council allocated its energy-efficiency budget among four categories in 2025. Overall, public buildings received the largest share, while research accounted for the smallest proportion. Public buildings and housing grants together represented a clear majority of the budget.

The allocation for public buildings was 40%, making it ten percentage points larger than the share for housing grants, which stood at 30%. Transport received 20% of the total. Consequently, the amount assigned to public buildings was twice the transport share. The smallest category was research, at 10%, exactly half the proportion allocated to transport.

When the two largest categories are combined, their share reaches 70%. This contrasts with the remaining 30% divided between transport and research. Housing grants alone received the same proportion as these two smaller categories together. All four percentages add up to the entire budget. However, because the chart reports proportions rather than the total amount available, it is not possible to determine the monetary value of any individual allocation.

writing.prompt: Many cities experience traffic congestion. What are the main causes, and what measures could address this problem?
writing.plan: Define your position and two main reasons. Plan one claim, explanation and example per body paragraph. Address the exact task and conclude without a new argument.
writing.model:
Traffic congestion results from several connected pressures, including concentrated travel demand and limited alternatives to private vehicles. Although building roads may help in specific locations, a lasting response should also make other forms of transport practical and reduce unnecessary peak-hour journeys.

A major cause is that many people travel to the same destinations at similar times. Schools and workplaces often begin together, producing demand that exceeds available road capacity. In addition, residents may choose cars because buses are unreliable or walking routes feel unsafe. In these circumstances, asking people to change their habits without improving their options is unlikely to work. A commuter who cannot depend on a bus arriving on time has a strong reason to continue driving.

One solution is to improve the reliability of public transport. Dedicated bus lanes, clear service information and convenient connections can make a journey more predictable. Cities can also create safer walking and cycling routes for shorter trips. These improvements should connect homes with actual destinations rather than form isolated sections. Meanwhile, employers can offer flexible starting times where the nature of the work allows it, spreading demand over a longer period.

Policies should be evaluated carefully. A road project may remove a bottleneck, but its cost and effects on neighbouring streets should be considered. Likewise, a new bus route is not successful merely because it exists; frequency and accessibility matter. In my view, cities should combine targeted infrastructure improvements with dependable alternatives and flexible travel arrangements. This approach addresses the reasons people drive while recognising that some journeys will still require private vehicles.

Receptionist: Community workshop bookings, good afternoon. How can I help?

Receptionist: That is exactly what our introductory course is designed for. We take people through measuring, marking and assembling a simple object. I will ask you a few questions and explain the arrangements before you decide.

listening.transcript:
Part 2. You will hear a talk in an everyday setting. Read questions 11 to 15. You have thirty seconds.

Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our visitor centre. I will explain the layout and the main arrangements before you explore independently. This is a small community building, not a large commercial attraction. Different rooms contain displays prepared by residents, and the grounds behind the building are used for outdoor activities. Please keep your group together during this introduction. Later you will be able to choose which displays interest you most and how long to spend at each one.

Guide: Our visitor centre opens at nine each morning, though staff arrive earlier.

Guide: You may see cleaners and delivery vehicles here before public access begins, but those early arrivals do not mean that visitors can enter. The published opening time applies every morning. On busy days we ask groups to wait outside while the reception team makes sure the routes are clear.

Guide: Walk past reception to the garden at the north end of the building.

Guide: For the plan questions, imagine you are standing at reception looking towards the top of your plan. The top is north. Follow the corridor straight ahead until you reach the glass doors. The outdoor growing area is beyond them, and you do not need to go upstairs.

Guide: The cafe is west of reception. The shop is east.

Guide: Remain at reception for the next direction. Your left-hand side corresponds to the west on this plan. One room offers food and drinks; the opposite room sells small gifts. Both can be entered directly from the central area. Do not confuse the two signs when you mark your plan.

Guide: The exhibition was designed by local students, not a commercial agency.

Guide: The team that prepared the exhibition interviewed older residents and selected objects representing everyday life. They completed the work alongside their studies. A professional firm advised on the lighting, but it did not create the displays. We wanted the exhibition to reflect what young people found interesting about their community.

Guide: The old photographs are copies. The originals remain in the archive.

Guide: Sensitive originals need more stable conditions than this busy display room provides. What you see on the wall has been reproduced so that visitors can look closely without risking damage. Requests to inspect original material must be made separately. Staff can tell you about the collection and the access procedure.

Now read questions 16 to 20. You have twenty seconds.

Guide: Visitors may take photographs, but flash is not allowed.

Guide: A picture taken with an ordinary camera is usually acceptable here. However, sudden intense light can distract visitors and affect delicate items. Please check the settings on your device before taking a photograph. If you are unsure about a particular display, ask the room attendant rather than guessing.

Guide: Guided walks leave every forty minutes.

Guide: A walk does not depart as soon as every new group arrives. Instead we follow a regular interval, which is displayed near reception. Guide: Borrow a waterproof jacket if you forgot yours. There is no charge.

Guide: We keep a small supply of spare clothing for people caught by a sudden change in weather. Borrowed items must be returned before you leave so they can be dried and used again. This is a courtesy service rather than a rental business, and you will not be asked for payment.

Guide: The feedback box is beside the exit. Please leave a comment.

Guide: Your comments help us improve access and decide which displays to develop. A short written suggestion is often more useful than a general rating. The collection point is placed where departing visitors naturally pass it. Please mention anything you enjoyed as well as anything that was confusing or difficult to find.

Part 3. You will hear a discussion in an educational setting. Read questions 21 to 25. You have thirty seconds.

Tutor: Let us look at the proposal for your introductory research project. I am not expecting a large professional study, but I do want a clear question and a method you can explain.
Student: We discussed several topics after the last class and have brought a revised plan. We also considered how to contact participants without interrupting their studies.
Tutor: Good. We will go through the topic, the collection method and the way you intend to compare the results. Keep a note of any decisions that replace your earlier ideas.

Tutor: Your topic was originally commuting. Student: We changed it to library use because the sample is easier to contact.

Tutor: The change makes sense if access is easier, but do not choose a topic only because it is convenient. What do you want to understand?
Student: We want to know how students use the study spaces and whether the facilities meet their needs. That is narrower than our original transport question.

Student: We will use a questionnaire rather than interviews for the first stage.

Student: Interviews might give detailed answers, but arranging individual appointments would take more time than we have. A written instrument lets people respond when convenient.
Tutor: That is reasonable for this stage. You can still include one short open response, provided you have a clear plan for analysing it.

Tutor: A long survey discourages responses. Keep it to ten questions.

listening.title: Lecture on urban food growing
listening.transcript:
Part 4. You will hear an academic lecture. Read questions 31 to 35. You have thirty seconds.

Lecturer: Today's lecture considers how small urban food-growing projects operate. We will use an invented neighbourhood case to examine decisions about resources, records and participation. The case is not evidence that every garden produces the same result. It is a way to separate the physical needs of growing plants from the organisational needs of a group. As you listen, note the factors that supported the project, the limitations that remained and the outcomes used in its evaluation.

Lecturer: Today we examine urban food growing. Land is important, but access to water often determines whether a project survives.

Lecturer: A vacant plot can appear suitable when viewed on a map, yet the practical supply of an essential resource may be difficult. Carrying heavy containers from a distant building is rarely sustainable for volunteers. Organisers therefore need to examine routine access before celebrating the availability of land. Ownership alone does not solve daily maintenance.

Lecturer: Raised beds can reduce contact with contaminated soil. They do not remove every risk.

Lecturer: The group did not assume that every part of the site was safe simply because weeds were growing there. They used a structure that separated the growing material from the underlying ground. Testing and advice were still necessary. A design can reduce exposure without turning an uncertain site into a completely risk-free place.

Lecturer: The fictional Oak Street project began with twelve households.

Lecturer: The initial group was small enough for members to discuss decisions together, but large enough to share regular jobs. New households joined later, so the starting figure should not be confused with participation at the end. In evaluating growth, we must distinguish between the number enrolled and the number attending a particular session.

Lecturer: Volunteers kept a diary of harvests rather than relying on memory.

Lecturer: Memory tends to favour unusually successful harvests and overlook disappointing ones. A written record made ordinary weeks visible as well. The volunteers noted what was collected and when, using a simple format that everyone could follow. The purpose was consistency, not creating a complicated administrative system that people would abandon.

Lecturer: Beans produced reliably, while tomatoes required more attention.

Lecturer: Different plants demanded different amounts of attention. One crop gave the group a dependable result, while another required more careful watering and protection. This distinction mattered because volunteers had limited time. A high yield under expert care may be less useful to a community group than a modest yield achieved consistently.

Now read questions 36 to 40. You have twenty seconds.

Lecturer: Shade from a neighbouring wall reduced the sunlight available.

Lecturer: Sunlight varied across the plot. The group had not noticed the full effect during its first visit, which took place at a different time of day. A nearby structure created a shaded area. Observing a site repeatedly can therefore reveal constraints that a quick inspection or a simple plan fails to show.

Lecturer: A shared compost area turned plant waste into a soil amendment.

Lecturer: Not everything removed from the beds had to leave the site. Appropriate plant material could be processed and returned to support later growing. The volunteers learned which materials belonged in the shared area and which did not. Clear signs and a regular maintenance rota prevented the facility from becoming an unmanaged pile of waste.

Lecturer: The group bought tools collectively to reduce costs.

Lecturer: Individual ownership would have meant several people purchasing the same equipment. A shared approach reduced duplication, although it introduced the need for storage and booking arrangements. The group labelled the equipment and agreed how to report damage. Saving money at purchase is helpful only if the items remain accessible and usable afterwards.

Lecturer: Participation declined in winter, when sessions were less frequent.

Lecturer: Attendance did not remain constant throughout the year. Cold conditions, shorter daylight and fewer organised sessions reduced opportunities to meet. That seasonal decline did not necessarily indicate permanent loss of interest. A fair evaluation should compare similar periods and consider the schedule, rather than treat every change as a judgement on the project.

Lecturer: The evaluation measured social contact as well as food production.

Lecturer: Food output was easy to count, but it was not the only reason residents took part. The evaluation also considered opportunities to meet neighbours and work together. These benefits required different measures from the harvest record. A project can be valuable in more than one way, and its assessment should reflect its stated purposes.

That is the end of Part 4. You have twenty seconds to check your answers.

listening.title: Booking a field course
listening.transcript:
Part 1. You will hear a conversation in an everyday setting. Read questions 1 to 5. You have thirty seconds.

Agent: University field-course office, hello.
Student: I would like to book the introductory course advertised on the noticeboard. I have checked my class schedule and can attend the whole trip. I am not sure which equipment is included, so I would appreciate some information before I pay.
Agent: Certainly. We will confirm the booking details first and then discuss travel and what you need to bring. The course takes place outdoors, so preparation matters even though no specialist experience is required.

Agent: What name shall I use? Student: Patel, spelled P A T E L.

Agent: We keep a list for the departure leader and a separate payment record. Spelling your name now helps us make both records consistent. You will receive a confirmation message later. Please check it carefully and tell us if the name is wrong rather than waiting until you board the bus.

Student: I considered geology but chose ecology.

Student: The first option sounded interesting, but it does not connect as closely with the module I am taking this term. I would like to observe living systems in the field.
Agent: That is a sensible reason for choosing. The two courses share transport arrangements but have different teaching activities once the groups reach the site.

Agent: The course begins on Monday, not Sunday.

Agent: Some older posters show a different departure day. Those were printed before the teaching schedule changed. The current booking form has the correct date, and the confirmation message will repeat it. Please use that information when arranging work or family commitments rather than relying on an old poster.

Agent: The bus leaves at seven fifteen in the morning.

Student: I will need to catch an early local service to campus.
Agent: Allow enough time to walk from the stop to the meeting point. The departure time means the bus should be moving then, not that students should begin arriving. The leader will check the attendance list before everyone boards.

Agent: The student fee is seventy-two pounds.

Agent: The student price covers transport and the field teaching. It does not include purchases you make independently during the trip.
Student: That is clear. I was comparing it with a residential course, which has accommodation included. This trip returns the same day, so the arrangements are different.

Now read questions 6 to 10. You have twenty seconds.

Agent: Meet at gate three beside the sports building.

Agent: There are several entrances to campus, and the usual main entrance is not where the group will meet. Look for the sports building and the numbered gate beside it. Staff will have a course sign. If you arrive at another entrance, ask the security team for directions rather than waiting there.

Agent: You must bring sturdy boots. Sandals are unsuitable.

Student: I have trainers and walking footwear at home.
Agent: Choose the sturdier option with good grip and protection around the ankle. The surface can be uneven and wet. Light open footwear would make the practical work uncomfortable and could be unsafe. We cannot lend footwear because sizes and fitting vary too much.

Student: Is lunch provided? Agent: No, please bring a packed lunch.

Student: I assumed there might be a cafe at the site.
Agent: There is a small one nearby, but opening cannot be guaranteed and we may be away from it during the break. Bring your own food in a bag you can carry easily. A reusable container is useful, and please take your rubbish home.

Agent: We will lend you binoculars for observing birds.

Agent: The specialist viewing equipment belongs to the department. We show you how to adjust it and ask that you handle it carefully.
Student: That is helpful, because I do not own any.
Agent: You do not need to buy it for this introductory course. Return borrowed equipment to the leader before the journey home.

Agent: Please confirm by email before Friday.

Agent: Use the written contact method so we have a record of your confirmation. Include your name and the course title.
Student: I will do that after checking the message you send.
Agent: Thank you. If there is an important change to travel arrangements, we will contact all confirmed participants using the details on their booking.

listening.transcript:
Part 2. You will hear a talk in an everyday setting. Read questions 11 to 15. You have thirty seconds.

Guide: Welcome to the learning centre. This orientation is for new members who will use our study rooms and practical facilities. I will describe the plan before explaining the access rules. On the plan, reception is in the middle and north is at the top. The ground floor has the main public spaces, while an additional activity room is upstairs. Please keep your membership documents with you today. Later visits will be quicker once staff have checked your details and explained how the equipment works.

Guide: The centre closes at eight in the evening on weekdays.

Guide: The weekday closing time is later than the weekend closing time. Do not assume that seeing lights inside means public study is still permitted, because cleaning staff remain afterwards. Announcements are made before closing so you can save your work and leave without rushing. Please check holiday arrangements separately.

Guide: Reception is central. The quiet room is east of it.

Guide: The room for silent individual study is on the right-hand side of reception when you face north. Its windows look towards the smaller courtyard. The entrance is clearly marked, but the corridor can be busy when classes finish. Conversation should stop before you enter so other members are not disturbed.

Guide: The computer lab is north of reception.

Guide: The room with desktop machines is directly ahead of reception on this plan. You will need to sign in before using a machine. Staff can help if you do not remember your account details. There are also sockets for personal devices elsewhere, but those areas should not be confused with the dedicated laboratory.

Guide: The stairs lead to a workshop on the first floor.

Guide: The upstairs activity space has benches rather than rows of study desks. Sessions there may involve making and testing objects, so it is not available for ordinary silent study during a class. Use the staircase only after checking the session arrangements. Members who need step-free access should speak to reception.

Guide: You need a card to use the lockers.

Guide: The storage system uses the same membership item that identifies you at the entrance. A cash deposit is not required, but you are responsible for returning the key. If your membership item is lost, tell staff immediately so it can be replaced and the old one can no longer be used.

Now read questions 16 to 20. You have twenty seconds.

Guide: Bags must remain in the lockers during practical sessions.

Guide: Practical rooms have limited clear floor space. Personal belongings should not be left beside benches where someone could trip over them or where equipment could damage them. The storage area is available before each session. Keep only the materials your instructor asks you to bring into the room.

Guide: Induction sessions last twenty minutes.

Guide: The introductory session is deliberately brief, but it covers essential safety and access information. It is not a substitute for instruction on each individual machine. If you arrive late, staff may ask you to attend another session rather than miss a rule that matters during practical work. Allow time for questions afterwards.

Guide: Please silence your phone in the quiet room.

Guide: Members sometimes think a device is silent because the ringtone has been turned off, then an alert interrupts the room. Check notifications as well as calls. If you must have a conversation, go to the designated social area. The silent room should remain suitable for people concentrating on demanding reading or writing.

Guide: A first-aid kit is kept behind reception.

Guide: Minor injuries should be reported even if they seem unimportant. Staff will help you locate the appropriate supplies and complete an incident record. The kit is kept where trained staff can reach it quickly, rather than in a classroom that may be locked. In an emergency, alert the nearest staff member first.

Guide: Suggestions can be entered on the website.

Guide: We collect suggestions through the online service because it allows us to organise them by facility and follow up when necessary. A specific description is useful: tell us where and when a problem occurred. You can also report urgent faults at the desk. Do not wait for a written response if equipment appears unsafe.
