listening.transcript:
Part 3. You will hear a discussion in an educational setting. Read questions 21 to 25. You have thirty seconds.

Tutor: Thank you for bringing your revised research proposal. Today we need to check that the population, the recording method and the timetable fit together.
Student: We were tempted to investigate a very broad question, but we realised we could not collect reliable information from everyone. We have narrowed the study and drafted instructions for volunteers.
Tutor: That is a useful start. We must also be careful about privacy and avoid treating a small student project as a medical assessment. Tell me what you have decided.

Tutor: Your question concerns sleep. Student: Yes, specifically sleep among first-year students.

Student: People starting university may still be adjusting to new routines, which makes the group relevant to our question.
Tutor: Explain that rationale rather than suggesting that every student has the same experience. You should state who is eligible and avoid drawing conclusions about people outside the population you actually studied.

Student: We plan to recruit eighty volunteers.

Student: We will advertise through the course mailing list and explain what participation involves before anyone agrees.
Tutor: Make sure your target is feasible. Some volunteers may withdraw or return incomplete records. Distinguish the number recruited from the number included in your final analysis, and give clear reasons for excluding any record.

Tutor: A diary may be better than asking people to remember an entire month.

Tutor: An immediate record is usually less dependent on distant recall.
Student: We can provide a simple form for each day rather than ask people to describe a whole month afterwards.
Tutor: Keep the format consistent. If participants invent their own categories, comparing records later may become difficult even when everyone is trying to be helpful.

Student: We will collect records over fourteen days.

Student: The collection period should include different sorts of days, but it must not become so long that people lose interest.
Tutor: Tell participants exactly when to begin and finish. Ask them to record missing days honestly rather than reconstructing them later. An incomplete record is easier to interpret than an invented entry.

Tutor: Record caffeine use, because it may affect sleep.

Tutor: The behaviour you are measuring can be affected by related habits, so the main record should include the agreed additional factor.
Student: We will ask for a simple description rather than expect volunteers to calculate complex quantities.
Tutor: State the limitations. The record will be self-reported and cannot establish a cause by itself.

Now read questions 26 to 30. You have twenty seconds.

Student: We will not ask participants for their names.

Student: We can assign a code to each volunteer, keeping the consent information separate from the daily record.
Tutor: That is preferable to collecting identifying details on every page. Explain who can access the information and how long you will keep it. Participants should know how to ask for their records to be removed.

Tutor: Make the instructions clear before the pilot.

Tutor: A technically correct instruction can still be difficult for a new volunteer to follow.
Student: We will use short sentences and show one completed example.
Tutor: Ask the pilot volunteers what they thought the instruction meant. Do not simply ask whether it was fine, because people may agree without describing a misunderstanding.

Student: The pilot will involve six volunteers.

Student: We have a small group willing to try the recording procedure before the main recruitment.
Tutor: That preliminary group is for testing the method, not proving your hypothesis. Review their comments and make the necessary changes. If you revise an item substantially, record the revision so the later report explains the final procedure accurately.

Tutor: Compare weekdays with weekends rather than merging them.

Tutor: The pattern may vary when classes are scheduled compared with the rest of the week.
Student: We will keep those periods separate rather than create only one combined figure.
Tutor: Good. The comparison should be planned before you inspect the results, otherwise you may be tempted to select whichever distinction looks most impressive.

Student: Our proposal deadline is the third of June.

listening.title: Lecture on preservation
listening.transcript:
Part 4. You will hear an academic lecture. Read questions 31 to 35. You have thirty seconds.

Lecturer: This lecture examines decisions made when preserving museum objects. The examples are fictional and simplify a complex professional field. The purpose is to understand how documentation, storage and access connect, not to provide treatment instructions. Different materials respond differently to the same environment, and an intervention that helps one object can harm another. We will follow the process from an initial record through environmental monitoring to the choice between displaying an original and providing a substitute for public use.

Lecturer: Preservation starts with documenting an object before treatment.

Lecturer: An object should not be altered before staff have an adequate record of its condition. Images, descriptions and relevant history create a baseline for later comparison. Without that baseline, a change discovered after treatment may be wrongly attributed to the treatment itself. The initial record also helps another specialist understand what was observed.

Lecturer: Light can damage some materials even when the room feels cool.

Lecturer: Visible comfort for people is not a reliable guide to every risk affecting a collection. A room can feel pleasant while a sensitive material is exposed to a damaging condition. Duration matters as well as intensity. A small exposure repeated for a long period can become significant, so monitoring must extend beyond obvious dramatic changes.

Lecturer: The fictional museum reduced the display period to six weeks.

Lecturer: The museum changed how long a fragile item remained on public view. This was a planned rotation, not evidence that the exhibition had failed. Other objects or reproductions filled the space afterwards. Visitors still had access to the subject, while the original spent more time in a carefully controlled storage environment.

Lecturer: Paper items were stored in protective folders.

Lecturer: Support and enclosure can protect a flat item from unnecessary handling, dust and movement. Storage materials must be appropriate to the object, rather than chosen only because they are cheap or convenient. Staff also need a system for locating items without repeatedly opening every container, which would increase handling and waste time.

Lecturer: Humidity was monitored daily, not just during exhibitions.

Lecturer: Environmental measurements were taken routinely, not only when a major display opened. This allowed staff to distinguish a brief fluctuation from a continuing problem. A record is useful only if somebody reviews it and acts when necessary. Collecting readings without interpreting them can give a false impression that a risk is being managed.

Now read questions 36 to 40. You have twenty seconds.

Lecturer: Staff used gloves when handling metal objects.

Lecturer: Handling procedures depended on the material. The protective item mentioned in the case reduced direct contact with a particular class of objects. It was not a universal instruction to use the same approach for everything. Staff followed the relevant guidance, supported delicate parts and avoided moving an object merely to satisfy curiosity.

Lecturer: Every treatment was recorded in a database.

Lecturer: A treatment record should be accessible to people who work with the collection later. A central electronic system helped connect condition information, interventions and location history. However, entering information once was not enough. Staff needed agreed terms and a method for correcting errors while retaining a record of important changes.

Lecturer: Repairs should be reversible where possible.

Lecturer: Future specialists may have better techniques or discover that an earlier assumption was wrong. Where possible, an intervention should allow that future reassessment. This principle does not mean that every repair can simply be removed without consequences. It means that long-term options should be considered rather than judging success only by immediate appearance.

Lecturer: A copy can allow access while protecting a fragile original.

Lecturer: Access and protection are sometimes presented as opposing goals, but a substitute can support both. Visitors may examine a reproduction closely while the vulnerable original remains protected. The substitute must be clearly identified so people are not misled. Its purpose is to provide access, not conceal the existence or condition of the original.

Lecturer: Preservation decisions involve values as well as technical knowledge.

Lecturer: Deciding what deserves preservation involves priorities, resources and the significance assigned to an object. Technical knowledge informs those decisions but does not make every value judgement disappear. A transparent explanation of priorities can help the public understand why one item is treated first or why access to another is temporarily restricted.

That is the end of Part 4. You have twenty seconds to check your answers.

listening.title: Volunteering at an event
listening.transcript:
Part 1. You will hear a conversation in an everyday setting. Read questions 1 to 5. You have thirty seconds.

Coordinator: Welcome to the event volunteer office. Are you calling about helping at the community open day?
Volunteer: Yes. I have attended before and would like to help this time. I am comfortable speaking to visitors, although I have not worked at the entrance desk.
Coordinator: We provide an introductory training session, so that is not a problem. Let us check your availability and preferences, then I will explain what happens when you arrive. Please ask if any part of the arrangement is unclear.

Coordinator: Can you spell your surname? Volunteer: Morgan, M O R G A N.

Coordinator: I will put your family name on the volunteer list. Please spell it so the person issuing identification can find you quickly.
Volunteer: Of course.
Coordinator: We do not need your full home address for this call. The confirmation message will explain the consent and emergency-contact information we collect before the event.

Volunteer: I prefer registration to serving refreshments.

Volunteer: I enjoy giving directions and checking people in. I would be less confident preparing food for a large group.
Coordinator: We try to place volunteers where they feel comfortable, although everyone may need to help with a simple unexpected task. Your main role will be the one we have agreed, and a supervisor will be nearby.

Coordinator: The event takes place on Saturday.

Coordinator: The public event is on the day stated in the current notice. The day before is reserved for staff setting up the rooms.
Volunteer: That suits my schedule. I was unsure whether volunteers had to attend both.
Coordinator: Only the scheduled training and the event itself are required for your role.

Coordinator: Please arrive at eight forty-five.

Coordinator: Your arrival time is earlier than the public opening because we need to brief the team and check that everyone has identification.
Volunteer: I will allow extra travel time.
Coordinator: If you are delayed, contact us rather than assuming you should miss the whole day. We may be able to adjust the rota.

Coordinator: Training lasts ninety minutes.

Volunteer: Will the training be a whole afternoon?
Coordinator: No. It is a focused introductory session covering visitor welcome, emergency procedures and when to refer a question to staff. You are not expected to memorise every detail of every activity. Knowing where to find reliable help is part of the role.

Now read questions 6 to 10. You have twenty seconds.

Coordinator: We expect two hundred visitors.

Coordinator: The attendance figure is an estimate based on bookings, not a promise that exactly that many people will arrive. Some visitors come without a reservation.
Volunteer: So we should be ready for the flow to change.
Coordinator: Yes. Keep the entrance clear and ask the supervisor before changing how the queue is organised.

Coordinator: Wear a blue shirt so visitors can identify you.

Coordinator: A consistent clothing colour helps people distinguish volunteers from visitors at a glance. The shirt does not need a printed logo. Choose something comfortable for moving between rooms.
Volunteer: I have one suitable for that.
Coordinator: Closed, comfortable footwear is also advisable, because you may be standing for part of the session.

Coordinator: You will receive a badge at the desk.

Volunteer: Should I make my own name label?
Coordinator: No, we issue the official identification at the desk. Wear it where visitors can see it, and return it when you finish. If you lose it during the day, report that immediately rather than borrowing somebody else's identification. Staff need to know who is present.

Coordinator: Lunch is provided, but bring your own water bottle.

Coordinator: We have arranged food for volunteers, but you should bring the item you need to carry drinking water during the day.
Volunteer: That is convenient.
Coordinator: Tell us in advance about dietary requirements. Do not assume a meal will meet a particular requirement unless the catering team has confirmed it.

Coordinator: Contact us by phone if you cannot attend.

Volunteer: If I become unwell, I will let you know rather than arrive and risk passing it on.
Coordinator: Please use the agreed contact method if you cannot attend, because it reaches the duty team quickly. The general website form may not be checked immediately. Thank you for offering your time; we will send the confirmation shortly.

listening.transcript:
Part 2. You will hear a talk in an everyday setting. Read questions 11 to 15. You have thirty seconds.

Guide: Welcome to the science park. Before the first demonstration I will describe the site and explain a few safety arrangements. Your plan has north at the top and a fountain in the centre. The main areas can be reached from that central point, so it is a useful place to meet if your group becomes separated. This is an outdoor learning space, and some activities depend on the weather. The staff will announce any change rather than expect you to guess from the equipment.

Guide: Our first demonstration begins at ten.

Guide: The first scheduled demonstration begins after staff have checked the equipment. Arriving at the park before that time does not mean the demonstration is already running. You can look at the introductory boards while you wait. Please gather at the marked meeting place when the guide makes the announcement.

Guide: The entrance is south of the central fountain.

Guide: When you look at the plan, the main way into the site is below the central fountain. Follow the path from that entrance directly towards the fountain. This gives you a consistent orientation for the direction questions. Do not rotate the plan mentally just because you are currently facing a different way.

Guide: The solar display is west of the fountain.

Guide: One energy display is to the left of the fountain on your plan. It uses sunlight, so its output varies with cloud cover. The demonstration explains that change rather than treating a lower reading as a fault. Please remain outside the marked equipment area even when the panel appears inactive.

Guide: The wind display is east of the fountain.

Guide: The other energy display is on the opposite side of the central feature. It responds to moving air rather than direct sunlight. Comparing the two can show why different systems vary over a day. You are welcome to ask questions, but do not try to turn or adjust the moving components yourself.

Guide: A covered shelter lies north of the fountain.

Guide: Above the fountain on the plan there is a covered place for groups to wait. It is useful when a short shower interrupts an activity. It is not the workshop or the shop, so please mark the correct function on your plan. Staff will tell you if a stronger weather warning requires leaving the site.

Now read questions 16 to 20. You have twenty seconds.

Guide: The workshop uses recycled materials.

Guide: The practical activity demonstrates that a useful model does not always require new materials. Items have been cleaned and checked before reuse. Participants should still inspect what they are given and tell the instructor about a sharp edge or damaged piece. The teaching aim is thoughtful design, not simply using every object available.

Guide: Children must remain with an adult near the pond.

Guide: The water area is part of the site but requires closer supervision than the open lawn. Younger visitors should not approach it independently. The person responsible for a child must remain close enough to intervene. A guide explaining a demonstration cannot simultaneously supervise every child in every part of the park.

Guide: The demonstration takes thirty minutes.

Guide: The demonstration has a fixed approximate length so the next group can begin on time. That period includes explanation and questions, not just the equipment operating. If you want a longer technical discussion, speak to staff afterwards without blocking the next group. We try to keep the programme accessible to visitors with different backgrounds.

Guide: The shop sells a booklet explaining the experiments.

Guide: A short printed explanation is available if you want to revisit the ideas at home. It describes the experiments and includes simple observations you can make safely. Purchasing it is optional, and you can enjoy the tour without it. Ask in the shop rather than at the demonstration area if you would like a copy.

Guide: The final tour leaves at four.

Guide: The last guided departure is earlier than the park's final closing time. This allows the group to finish without rushing. Visitors arriving later may still view the outdoor boards but cannot join a tour that has already left. Check the departure notice before spending a long time in the shop or at the entrance.

That is the end of Part 2. You have twenty seconds to check your answers.

Student: We have revised our transport survey and would like your advice on the observation schedule.
Tutor: Tell me how you will make the comparison fair. A simple project can still be useful if the conditions and limitations are clearly described.
Student: We decided not to compare every possible form of transport. We chose a pair that students commonly use for short journeys to campus.
Tutor: Good. We will review the routes, the measurement procedure and the final presentation. Keep track of the decisions we make today.

Student: Our project compares cycling with walking to campus.

Student: The two activities have different speeds but can both be used without waiting for a scheduled service.
Tutor: Define the beginning and end of each journey consistently. If one measurement starts at a door and another starts halfway along the route, the figures will not describe a fair comparison.

Tutor: Select three routes with different traffic levels.

Tutor: Your routes should provide a meaningful contrast without creating a project too large to manage.
Student: We have selected a small number with different traffic conditions.
Tutor: Describe why each was chosen. You are not claiming that this small selection represents every road in the city, so be careful about the scope of your conclusion.

Student: We will observe each route for seven days.

Student: We want to observe repeatedly instead of judging each route from one journey.
Tutor: A fixed collection period is helpful, but you should still report unusual events. Roadworks or a major event could affect a day. Do not quietly discard an inconvenient observation merely because it makes the pattern less tidy.

Tutor: Record weather as well as travel time.

Tutor: Conditions outside the traveller's control can affect both comfort and journey time.
Student: We will record the agreed contextual factor alongside the timing.
Tutor: Use simple consistent categories and make the observation at the time of the journey. A record reconstructed afterwards may miss a change that affected one route but not another.

Student: We will use a stopwatch instead of phone estimates.

Student: We tried using an application, but different devices produced slightly different estimates.
Tutor: Use the same direct timing method for the main comparison. Agree on exactly when to start and stop it. Practise the procedure during the pilot, and record interruptions rather than trying to remove them from memory later.

Now read questions 26 to 30. You have twenty seconds.

Tutor: Include morning journeys and evening journeys.

Tutor: Travel conditions can differ across the day. If you collect only one period, your conclusion should be limited to that period.
Student: We can include journeys at the other agreed time as well.
Tutor: Keep the periods identifiable in the data. Averaging everything too early can hide a useful difference.

Student: Our pilot includes eight participants.

Student: The pilot group is small but includes people unfamiliar with our recording form.
Tutor: That will help reveal unclear instructions. The pilot is a test of the procedure, not a second study to combine automatically with your final sample. Decide how you will use its comments before collecting the main observations.

Tutor: Ask permission before photographing people.

Tutor: Visual records can be useful, but other people may not expect to become part of a student project.
Student: We will ask first and avoid taking identifiable pictures when consent is unclear.
Tutor: Good. Your project should not interfere with traffic or encourage participants to take risks just to obtain an interesting image.

Student: We want an audience to compare the main findings at a glance rather than wait through a sequence of slides.
Tutor: The format you have chosen suits that purpose. Include the method and limitations as well as the most attractive chart. A clear presentation should allow someone to understand what the numbers do and do not show.

Tutor: Submit the report on the twenty-first of July.

Tutor: Leave time to check that the report and the visual presentation use the same figures.
Student: We will work backwards from the submission date and complete analysis before the final week.
Tutor: That is sensible. If the collection method changes, explain the change in the report instead of pretending the original plan was followed exactly.

listening.title: Lecture on communication
listening.transcript:
Part 4. You will hear an academic lecture. Read questions 31 to 35. You have thirty seconds.

Lecturer: Today we consider communication within a team whose members have different professional backgrounds. Our fictional case brings together an engineer, an administrator and other staff responsible for a shared project. They use some of the same words but do not always interpret those words in the same way. We will examine how examples, discussion and revision helped expose these differences. The aim is not to suggest that every meeting needs a lengthy language exercise, but to understand when clarification can prevent a more expensive misunderstanding later.

Lecturer: Communication depends on shared meaning, not merely repeated words.

Lecturer: Repeating a term louder or more often does not guarantee that the listener attaches the same idea to it. The group initially assumed agreement because nobody objected. A practical decision later revealed that members had understood the instruction differently. Successful communication therefore needs more than the transmission of a recognisable expression.

Lecturer: Our fictional team used examples beside definitions.

Lecturer: A short formal definition gave the team a starting point, but it did not show how the term would operate in a real decision. The added illustrations connected abstract language to a concrete situation. Members could discuss the illustration and discover where their interpretations diverged, rather than merely agree that the definition sounded reasonable.

Lecturer: Participants worked in four small groups.

Lecturer: The workshop divided participants into manageable units. The number was chosen so that each person had an opportunity to contribute while the facilitator could still compare outcomes. A single large conversation had allowed more confident members to dominate. Smaller units did not remove every inequality, but they made overlooked interpretations easier to hear.

Lecturer: Each group discussed a different scenario.

Lecturer: Each unit worked with a particular imagined situation. The situations were related to the project but were not identical, which allowed the facilitator to compare how the same terms were applied in different circumstances. This method exposed assumptions that a purely general discussion had left hidden. Groups reported the reasoning behind their decisions, not just a final choice.

Lecturer: Paraphrasing revealed assumptions that repetition concealed.

Lecturer: Restating an idea in different language forced participants to reveal what they thought it meant. Simple repetition had concealed that reasoning. The facilitator asked another member to explain the idea back without copying the original wording. This was not a test of elegant speech; it was a way of checking that the intended concept had been understood.

Now read questions 36 to 40. You have twenty seconds.

Lecturer: The engineer focused on energy use.

Lecturer: The technical specialist interpreted efficiency mainly through a physical resource used by the system. That interpretation made sense within the specialist's work, but it was not the only meaning relevant to the team. The discussion showed why a proposal could look efficient to one member and still appear problematic to another.

Lecturer: The administrator focused on time.

Lecturer: The administrative specialist approached the same term through a different resource associated with scheduling and completing tasks. Neither interpretation was automatically wrong. The difficulty arose when the team used one word as if it guaranteed one shared measure. They needed to specify which measure applied to each decision instead of relying on an apparently simple label.

Lecturer: Notes retained unresolved questions.

Lecturer: The meeting record did not pretend that every issue had been settled. Items needing further work were kept visible so that someone could investigate them. This was preferable to recording a false consensus. Each unresolved item was assigned a responsible person, and the next meeting began by reviewing what had been learned.

Lecturer: The glossary was revised monthly.

Lecturer: The shared list of terms was not treated as a document that could be completed once and forgotten. Scheduled revision allowed members to add examples and correct descriptions that no longer matched the work. The interval was regular enough to keep the document useful without requiring a new version after every small conversation.

Lecturer: Clarification has a cost, but ambiguity can create larger delays.

Lecturer: Time spent checking an interpretation can look inefficient during a busy meeting. However, an unclear instruction may cause rework, missed responsibilities or incompatible decisions. The case therefore compared the immediate effort of clarification with the later effects of leaving uncertainty unresolved. The most efficient choice is not always the one that ends the conversation fastest.

That is the end of Part 4. You have twenty seconds to check your answers.

units.context: Question: Do you enjoy cooking? Response: Yes, because preparing dinner helps me relax after work.
units.question: What detail extends the direct answer?
units.answer: helps me relax after work|preparing dinner helps me relax after work
units.explanation: The response extends Yes with a personal reason.
units.strategy: Practise short natural answers rather than memorised speeches.
units.mistake: Choosing a related detail instead of answering the exact question.

uploadedPractice.title: Future plans
uploadedPractice.question: Think about your own future. Write four important plans that you have. Think about:

uploadedPractice.title: Opening a Restaurant
uploadedPractice.question: Group Planning Task: “Opening a Restaurant”
points: Restaurant Name: What will you call your restaurant? Is the name attractive and easy to remember?
Theme & Concept: What type of restaurant will it be? (e.g., fast food, traditional, international, café style)
Location: Where will you open it? (city center, near school/college, riverside, shopping mall)
Menu & Food Items: What kind of food will you serve? (local dishes, burgers & pizza, desserts, healthy food)
Target Customers: Who are your main customers? (students, families, office workers, tourists)
Budget & Cost: How much money will you need to start? How will you share the cost with friends?
Staff & Roles: How many staff will you need? Who will cook, serve, manage, or do marketing?
Marketing Plan: How will you promote your restaurant? (social media, posters, discounts, opening event)
Special Features: What makes your restaurant unique? (live music, rooftop, free Wi-Fi, kids’ zone)
Future Goals: If successful, how will you expand? (more branches, online delivery, new menu items)
